exercises.title: Inverses in 𝔽₅
exercises.description: Determine in $\mathbb{F}_5 = \mathbb{Z}_5$ the multiplicative inverses of all non-zero elements and solve $3x + 2 = 4$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In a field one may “divide” by every non-zero element, i.e. multiply by its inverse. In $\mathbb{F}_5$ one looks for $b$ with $ab \equiv 1 \pmod 5$ for each $a$.

Step 3: Solve the equation
$3x + 2 = 4 \iff 3x = 2$. Multiplying by $3^{-1} = 2$: $x = 2\cdot2 = 4$.

Step 4: Check
$3\cdot4 + 2 = 14 \equiv 4 \pmod 5$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Linear equations can be solved in any field as usual. Uniqueness of the solution follows from the absence of zero divisors.

exercises.title: Is ℤ₈ a field?
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Z}_8$ is not a field and determine which elements are invertible.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A field requires that every non-zero element is invertible. A single non-invertible non-zero element suffices.

Step 2: Non-invertible element
$2$ has no inverse: $2\cdot x$ is always even and so can never be $1$ modulo $8$. Moreover $2\cdot4 = 8 \equiv 0$: $2$ is a zero divisor.

Step 3: All units
$a$ is invertible $\iff \gcd(a,8) = 1$, so $a \in \{1,3,5,7\}$ (e.g. $3\cdot3 = 9 \equiv 1$, $5\cdot5 = 25 \equiv 1$, $7\cdot7 = 49 \equiv 1$).

Step 4: Conclusion
The elements $2,4,6$ are not invertible, so $\mathbb{Z}_8$ is not a field (only a commutative ring). A field with $8$ elements does exist nevertheless: $\mathbb{F}_8 = \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^3+x+1)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
A field with $q$ elements exists exactly when $q$ is a prime power; $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field only for prime $n$.

exercises.title: Determining the characteristic
exercises.description: Determine the characteristic of $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Z}_7$ and $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The **characteristic** of a field is the smallest $n \geq 1$ with $\underbrace{1 + \dots + 1}_{n} = 0$; if none exists the characteristic is $0$.

Step 2: $\mathbb{Q}$
$1 + \dots + 1 = n \neq 0$ for all $n \geq 1$. Characteristic $0$.

Step 3: $\mathbb{Z}_7$
$7\cdot1 = 0$ and no smaller $n$ works. Characteristic $7$.

Step 4: $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$
The identity is $1 \in \mathbb{F}_2$, and $1 + 1 = 0$ already in $\mathbb{F}_2$. Characteristic $2$ (the field has $4$ elements).

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
The characteristic of a field is $0$ or a prime $p$. A finite field always has positive characteristic $p$ and $p^n$ elements.

exercises.title: Computing in ℚ(√2)
exercises.description: Compute in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ the product $(1+\sqrt2)(3-\sqrt2)$ and the inverse of $1+\sqrt2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The elements of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ have the form $a + b\sqrt2$ with $a,b \in \mathbb{Q}$; one computes with $\sqrt2^2 = 2$. The inverse is obtained by expanding with the conjugate (third binomial formula).

Step 2: Product
$(1+\sqrt2)(3-\sqrt2) = 3 - \sqrt2 + 3\sqrt2 - 2 = 1 + 2\sqrt2$.

Step 3: Inverse
$\frac{1}{1+\sqrt2} = \frac{1-\sqrt2}{(1+\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt2)} = \frac{1-\sqrt2}{1 - 2} = \sqrt2 - 1$.

Step 4: Check
$(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt2 - 1) = \sqrt2 - 1 + 2 - \sqrt2 = 1$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
The denominator $a^2 - 2b^2$ is $0$ only if $a = b = 0$ because $\sqrt2$ is irrational — that is why every non-zero element is invertible. $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ is a field, $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ only a ring.

exercises.title: The field 𝔽₄
exercises.description: Let $\mathbb{F}_4 = \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$ with elements $0, 1, \omega, \omega+1$ where $\omega^2 = \omega+1$. Compute $\omega\cdot\omega$, $\omega\cdot(\omega+1)$ and the inverses of $\omega$ and $\omega + 1$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In $\mathbb{F}_2$ we have $1 + 1 = 0$, so $-1 = 1$. From $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$ we get $\omega^2 = -\omega - 1 = \omega + 1$. This reduces every product to the form $a + b\omega$.

Step 2: $\omega\cdot\omega$
$\omega^2 = \omega + 1$.

Step 3: $\omega(\omega+1)$
$\omega(\omega+1) = \omega^2 + \omega = (\omega+1) + \omega = 2\omega + 1 = 1$.

Step 4: Inverses
From $\omega(\omega+1) = 1$ we get $\omega^{-1} = \omega + 1$ and $(\omega+1)^{-1} = \omega$.

Step 5: Multiplicative group
$\omega^2 = \omega+1$, $\omega^3 = \omega\cdot(\omega+1) = 1$: $\mathbb{F}_4^\times = \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ is cyclic of order $3$ with generator $\omega$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Every field with $4$ elements is (up to isomorphism) this field; it is **not** $\mathbb{Z}_4$ (there $2\cdot2 = 0$). The multiplicative group of a finite field is always cyclic.

exercises.title: Verifying Field Axioms
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}] = \{a + b\sqrt{2} \mid a,b \in \mathbb{Q}\}$ with the usual addition and multiplication forms a field.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Ring Properties
$\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}]$ is a ring (as shown in the ring exercise).

Step 2: Commutativity of Multiplication
$(a + b\sqrt{2}) \cdot (c + d\sqrt{2}) = (c + d\sqrt{2}) \cdot (a + b\sqrt{2})$
Multiplication is commutative.

Step 3: Existence of Inverses
For $a + b\sqrt{2} \neq 0$:
$(a + b\sqrt{2})^{-1} = \frac{a - b\sqrt{2}}{a^2 - 2b^2} \in \mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}]$
The denominator is never 0, since $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

Step 4: Conclusion
$\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{2}]$ satisfies all field axioms and is thus a field.

exercises.title: Field Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ is a field extension of degree 2 over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Basis of the Extension
$\{1,\sqrt{2}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

Step 2: Linear Independence
Suppose $a + b\sqrt{2} = 0$.
Then $a = b = 0$ due to the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$.

Step 3: Generating System
Every element can be expressed as a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination.

Step 4: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$.

exercises.title: Characteristic
exercises.description: Determine the characteristic of the field $\mathbb{Z}_5$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Definition
The characteristic is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $n \cdot 1 = 0$.

Step 2: Calculation
$1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
$2 \cdot 1 = 2$.
$3 \cdot 1 = 3$.
$4 \cdot 1 = 4$.
$5 \cdot 1 = 0$.

Step 3: Conclusion
The characteristic of $\mathbb{Z}_5$ is 5.

exercises.title: Field Homomorphisms
exercises.description: Show that the map $\varphi: \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}) \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ with $\varphi(a + b\sqrt{2}) = a - b\sqrt{2}$ is a field homomorphism.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Additivity
$\varphi((a + b\sqrt{2}) + (c + d\sqrt{2})) = \varphi((a+c) + (b+d)\sqrt{2}) = (a+c) - (b+d)\sqrt{2} = (a - b\sqrt{2}) + (c - d\sqrt{2}) = \varphi(a + b\sqrt{2}) + \varphi(c + d\sqrt{2})$.

Step 2: Multiplicativity
$\varphi((a + b\sqrt{2}) \cdot (c + d\sqrt{2})) = \varphi((ac + 2bd) + (ad + bc)\sqrt{2}) = (ac + 2bd) - (ad + bc)\sqrt{2} = (a - b\sqrt{2}) \cdot (c - d\sqrt{2}) = \varphi(a + b\sqrt{2}) \cdot \varphi(c + d\sqrt{2})$.

Step 3: Bijectivity
$\varphi$ is bijective with $\varphi^{-1} = \varphi$.

Step 4: Conclusion
$\varphi$ is a field automorphism.

exercises.title: Finite Field Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{F}_4$ is a field extension of degree 2 over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construction
$\mathbb{F}_4 = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(X^2 + X + 1)$.

Step 2: Basis
$\{1,X\}$ is an $\mathbb{F}_2$-basis.

Step 3: Linear Independence
$\{1,X\}$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

Step 4: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{F}_4:\mathbb{F}_2] = 2$.

exercises.title: Determining a minimal polynomial
exercises.description: Determine the minimal polynomial of $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt3$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and the degree of $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of smallest degree in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ having $\alpha$ as a root. We isolate the root and square to eliminate it.

Step 2: Isolate the root
$\alpha - 1 = \sqrt3$. Squaring: $(\alpha-1)^2 = 3$.

Step 3: Set up the polynomial
$\alpha^2 - 2\alpha + 1 - 3 = 0$, so $\alpha$ is a root of $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 2$.

Step 4: Irreducibility
The roots of $f$ are $1 \pm \sqrt3 \notin \mathbb{Q}$. A degree-$2$ polynomial without rational root is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. So $f$ is the minimal polynomial.

Step 5: Degree of the extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = \deg f = 2$. We have $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)$ with basis $\{1, \sqrt3\}$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The degree of the extension is the degree of the minimal polynomial. Irreducibility over $\mathbb{Q}$ is checked by roots for small degree, later with Eisenstein's criterion.

exercises.title: Inverse in ℚ(∛2)
exercises.description: Let $a = \sqrt[3]{2}$. Determine the inverse of $1 + a$ in $\mathbb{Q}(a)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Elements of $\mathbb{Q}(a)$ have the form $c_0 + c_1a + c_2a^2$ (basis $1,a,a^2$ since $a^3 = 2$). The inverse is found with the sum formula $(1 + a)(1 - a + a^2) = 1 + a^3$.

Step 2: Sum-of-cubes formula
$(1 + a)(1 - a + a^2) = 1 - a + a^2 + a - a^2 + a^3 = 1 + a^3 = 1 + 2 = 3$.

Step 3: Read off the inverse
Dividing by $3$: $(1 + a)\cdot\frac{1 - a + a^2}{3} = 1$. So $(1+a)^{-1} = \frac13(1 - a + a^2)$.

Step 4: Numerical check
$a \approx 1.26$: $1 + a \approx 2.26$; $\frac13(1 - 1.26 + 1.587) \approx \frac13\cdot1.327 \approx 0.4425$; $2.26\cdot0.4425 \approx 1.0$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
General principle: in $K[a]/(m(a))$ inverses are found via factorisations or the extended Euclidean algorithm for polynomials. Here $x^3 + 1 = (x+1)(x^2 - x + 1)$ helps.

exercises.title: Inverse in 𝔽₉
exercises.description: Let $\mathbb{F}_9 = \mathbb{F}_3[x]/(x^2+1)$. Compute $(1+x)^2$, the order of $1 + x$ and the inverse of $2 + x$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We compute with $x^2 = -1 = 2$ and coefficients modulo $3$. The elements have the form $a + bx$ with $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}_3$.

Step 3: Order of $1+x$
$(1+x)^2 = 2x$, $(1+x)^4 = (2x)^2 = 4x^2 = x^2 = -1$, $(1+x)^8 = 1$. The order is $8$ (since $(1+x)^4 = -1 \neq 1$): $1 + x$ generates the multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_9^\times$ of order $8$.

Step 4: Inverse of $2+x$
Ansatz $(2+x)(a+bx) = 2a + (a+2b)x + bx^2 = (2a - b) + (a + 2b)x = 1$. So $a + 2b = 0$ and $2a - b = 1$. From $a = -2b = b$: $2b - b = b = 1$, $a = 1$. Inverse: $1 + x$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ is cyclic of order $q - 1$; a generator is called a **primitive element**. The order of every element divides $q - 1 = 8$.

exercises.title: Field homomorphisms are injective
exercises.description: Show: every field homomorphism $\varphi: K \to L$ is injective. Determine all field homomorphisms $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2) \to \mathbb{R}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal. A field has only the ideals $\{0\}$ and $K$. Because $\varphi(1) = 1 \neq 0$ the kernel cannot be all of $K$.

Step 2: Injectivity
Let $a \in \ker\varphi$, $a \neq 0$. Then $1 = \varphi(a a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = 0\cdot\varphi(a^{-1}) = 0$, a contradiction. So $\ker\varphi = \{0\}$ and $\varphi$ is injective.

Step 3: Image of $\sqrt2$
A field homomorphism fixes $\mathbb{Q}$ and preserves the equation $\sqrt2^2 = 2$: $\varphi(\sqrt2)^2 = 2$, so $\varphi(\sqrt2) = \pm\sqrt2$.

Step 4: The two homomorphisms
$\varphi_+(a + b\sqrt2) = a + b\sqrt2$ (identity) and $\varphi_-(a + b\sqrt2) = a - b\sqrt2$ (conjugation). Both preserve sum and product: $(a+b\sqrt2)(c+d\sqrt2) = (ac + 2bd) + (ad+bc)\sqrt2$ is conjugated to $(a-b\sqrt2)(c-d\sqrt2)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
There are exactly as many homomorphisms as the minimal polynomial has roots in the target field: $x^2 - 2$ has two real roots $\pm\sqrt2$. This idea leads directly to Galois theory.

exercises.title: Existence of finite fields
exercises.description: Decide for which element counts $6, 8, 9, 10, 12$ a finite field exists and give a short justification each.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A finite field has positive characteristic $p$ (prime) and is a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$ of dimension $n$. So it has $p^n$ elements: the element count is a **prime power**.

Step 2: Prime powers
$8 = 2^3$ and $9 = 3^2$ are prime powers: there are fields $\mathbb{F}_8$ and $\mathbb{F}_9$.

Step 3: Not prime powers
$6 = 2\cdot3$, $10 = 2\cdot5$, $12 = 2^2\cdot3$ have at least two different prime divisors. So there is **no** field with $6$, $10$ or $12$ elements.

Step 4: Constructions
$\mathbb{F}_8 = \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^3+x+1)$ ($x^3 + x + 1$ has no root in $\mathbb{F}_2$ and is therefore irreducible); $\mathbb{F}_9 = \mathbb{F}_3[x]/(x^2+1)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
For every prime power $q = p^n$ there is **exactly one** finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ (up to isomorphism). $\mathbb{Z}_8$ is **not** $\mathbb{F}_8$ (zero divisors!).

exercises.title: Finite Fields
exercises.description: Construct a field with 4 elements and provide its addition and multiplication tables.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construction
$\mathbb{F}_4 = \mathbb{Z}_2[X]/(X^2 + X + 1)$
Elements: $\{0,1,X,X+1\}$.

Step 2: Addition Table
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}
+ & 0 & 1 & X & X+1 \\\hline
0 & 0 & 1 & X & X+1 \\
1 & 1 & 0 & X+1 & X \\
X & X & X+1 & 0 & 1 \\
X+1 & X+1 & X & 1 & 0
\end{array}$

Step 3: Multiplication Table
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\cdot & 0 & 1 & X & X+1 \\\hline
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 1 & X & X+1 \\
X & 0 & X & X+1 & 1 \\
X+1 & 0 & X+1 & 1 & X
\end{array}$

Step 4: Verification
- $X^2 = X+1$ (since $X^2 + X + 1 = 0$).
- Every non-zero element has an inverse.
- The distributive laws hold.

exercises.title: Algebraic Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ is an algebraic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ and determine the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Minimal Polynomial
$f(X) = X^3 - 2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2}$.

Step 2: Irreducibility
By the Eisenstein criterion with $p=2$, $f$ is irreducible.

Step 3: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$.

Step 4: Basis
$\{1,\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{4}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

exercises.title: Algebraic Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2})$ is an algebraic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ and determine the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[4]{2}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Minimal Polynomial
$f(X) = X^4 - 2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[4]{2}$.

Step 2: Irreducibility
By the Eisenstein criterion with $p=2$, $f$ is irreducible.

Step 3: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$.

Step 4: Basis
$\{1,\sqrt[4]{2},\sqrt{2},\sqrt[4]{8}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

exercises.title: Field Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{5})$ is a field extension of degree 8 over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Basis of the Extension
$\{1,\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{5},\sqrt{6},\sqrt{10},\sqrt{15},\sqrt{30}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

Step 2: Linear Independence
The elements are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Step 3: Generating System
Every element can be expressed as a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination.

Step 4: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{5}):\mathbb{Q}] = 8$.

exercises.title: Field Homomorphisms
exercises.description: Determine all field homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$ to $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Identity
$\varphi_1(a + b\sqrt{3}) = a + b\sqrt{3}$.

Step 2: Conjugation
$\varphi_2(a + b\sqrt{3}) = a - b\sqrt{3}$.

Step 3: Verification
Both maps are field homomorphisms.

Step 4: Conclusion
$\text{Aut}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})) = \{\varphi_1,\varphi_2\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$.

exercises.title: Field Extensions and Minimal Polynomials
exercises.description: Determine the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Calculation
$(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3})^2 = 5 + 2\sqrt{6}$.
$(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3})^4 = 49 + 20\sqrt{6}$.

Step 2: Minimal Polynomial
$f(X) = X^4 - 10X^2 + 1$.

Step 3: Irreducibility
$f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Step 4: Conclusion
$f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.

exercises.title: The Frobenius homomorphism
exercises.description: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Prove $(a+b)^p = a^p + b^p$ and conclude that $\varphi(x) = x^p$ is a field homomorphism. If $K$ is finite, $\varphi$ is an automorphism.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The binomial theorem gives $(a+b)^p = \sum_{k=0}^p \binom pk a^{p-k}b^k$. We show that the middle binomial coefficients are divisible by $p$ and hence vanish in characteristic $p$.

Step 2: Divisibility of the coefficients
For $0 < k < p$ we have $\binom pk = \frac{p!}{k!(p-k)!}$. The numerator contains the factor $p$, the denominator does not (all factors $< p$). Since $\binom pk$ is an integer, $p \mid \binom pk$.

Step 3: Additivity
In $K$ we have $p\cdot1 = 0$, so $\binom pk\cdot a^{p-k}b^k = 0$ for $0 < k < p$. What remains is $(a+b)^p = a^p + b^p$.

Step 4: Multiplicativity and identity
$(ab)^p = a^pb^p$ (commutative) and $1^p = 1$. So $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism and hence (field) injective.

Step 5: Finite fields
If $K$ is finite, the injective map $\varphi: K \to K$ is also surjective. So $\varphi$ is an automorphism. Example $K = \mathbb{F}_9$: $\varphi$ swaps the roots $x$ and $x^3 = -x$ of $x^2 + 1$. $\blacksquare$

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
On the prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, $\varphi$ is the identity (Fermat's little theorem: $a^p = a$). The Frobenius map generates the Galois group of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p$, which is cyclic of order $n$.

exercises.title: Minimal polynomial of √2 + √3
exercises.description: Determine the minimal polynomial of $\alpha = \sqrt2 + \sqrt3$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and show $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We eliminate the roots by squaring twice and show that the resulting degree-$4$ polynomial is irreducible. The root $\sqrt2$ is separated from the root $\sqrt3$.

Step 2: First squaring
$\alpha - \sqrt2 = \sqrt3 \Rightarrow \alpha^2 - 2\sqrt2\alpha + 2 = 3$, so $\alpha^2 - 1 = 2\sqrt2\alpha$.

Step 3: Second squaring
$(\alpha^2 - 1)^2 = 8\alpha^2 \Rightarrow \alpha^4 - 2\alpha^2 + 1 = 8\alpha^2 \Rightarrow \alpha^4 - 10\alpha^2 + 1 = 0$.

Step 4: Irreducibility
$f(x) = x^4 - 10x^2 + 1$ has the roots $\pm\sqrt2 \pm \sqrt3$ (all irrational). A factorisation into two quadratic factors needs checking: with the ansatz $(x^2 + ax + b)(x^2 - ax + c)$ all cases lead to contradictions (for $b = c$ we get $a^2 = 8$ or $a^2 = 12$ — no rational squares; for $a = 0$ the numbers $b,c$ would have sum $-10$ and product $1$, discriminant $96$ is not a square).

Step 5: Degree
So $f$ is the minimal polynomial and $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$. Since $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ and $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$ we get $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ (primitive element).

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The example shows the primitive element theorem: the extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb{Q}$ is generated by a **single** element. The four roots of $f$ are exactly the images of $\alpha$ under the four automorphisms.

exercises.title: Irreducibility of x⁴ + x + 1 over 𝔽₂
exercises.description: Show that $f = x^4 + x + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and conclude that $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(f)$ is a field with $16$ elements.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A polynomial of degree $4$ is reducible if it has a root (linear factor) or splits into two irreducible quadratic factors. We check both cases.

Step 2: No roots
$f(0) = 1$ and $f(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 1$. Both values are $\neq 0$: no linear factor.

Step 3: Quadratic factors
The only irreducible degree-$2$ polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is $x^2 + x + 1$ (the others $x^2$, $x^2+x$, $x^2+1$ have roots). If $f$ split into two quadratic factors, we would have $f = (x^2+x+1)^2 = x^4 + x^2 + 1$.

Step 4: Comparison
$x^4 + x^2 + 1 \neq x^4 + x + 1$, so there is no such factorisation. Hence $f$ is irreducible.

Step 5: The field $\mathbb{F}_{16}$
$(f)$ is maximal, so $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(f)$ is a field. Its elements are $a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3$ with $a_i \in \mathbb{F}_2$: $2^4 = 16$ elements, computed with $x^4 = x + 1$. $\blacksquare$

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The root test alone is not enough from degree $4$ on. This $f$ is a **primitive** polynomial: $x$ has order $15$ and so generates the multiplicative group of the field. Such fields are used in coding theory (BCH, Reed–Solomon).

exercises.title: Galois group of ℚ(√2) and fixed field
exercises.description: Determine the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)/\mathbb{Q})$ and the fixed field of the non-trivial map.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A $\mathbb{Q}$-automorphism of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ is determined by the image of $\sqrt2$. This image must be a root of the minimal polynomial $x^2 - 2$.

Step 2: Possible images
$\sigma(\sqrt2)^2 = \sigma(2) = 2$, so $\sigma(\sqrt2) \in \{\sqrt2, -\sqrt2\}$.

Step 3: The automorphisms
$\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma: a + b\sqrt2 \mapsto a - b\sqrt2$. Both are bijective and preserve sum and product. Since $\sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}$ we get $\operatorname{Aut} = \{\mathrm{id},\sigma\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$.

Step 4: Fixed field
$\sigma(a + b\sqrt2) = a + b\sqrt2 \iff -b\sqrt2 = b\sqrt2 \iff b = 0$. The fixed field is $\mathbb{Q}$.

Step 5: Norm and trace
For $z = a + b\sqrt2$ we have $z\sigma(z) = a^2 - 2b^2 \in \mathbb{Q}$ (norm) and $z + \sigma(z) = 2a \in \mathbb{Q}$ (trace).

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Special case of the fundamental theorem: $|\operatorname{Gal}| = [\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$ and the fixed field of the Galois group is the base field. The conjugation $\sigma$ explains why denominators are expanded with the conjugate.

exercises.title: Cyclicity of the multiplicative group
exercises.description: Show that $3$ is a generator of the multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_7^\times$ and determine all generators.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The group $\mathbb{F}_7^\times$ has order $6$. An element $g$ is a generator if its order is $6$, i.e. if neither $g^2$ nor $g^3$ equals $1$ (the proper divisors of $6$ are $1,2,3$).

Step 3: Generator
$3$ has order $6$ and generates $\mathbb{F}_7^\times$: it is cyclic, isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_6$.

Step 4: All generators
The generators are $3^k$ with $\gcd(k,6) = 1$, so $k \in \{1,5\}$: $3^1 = 3$ and $3^5 = 5$. There are $\varphi(6) = 2$ generators: $\{3,5\}$.

Step 5: Counter-check $2$
$2^3 = 8 \equiv 1$: $2$ has only order $3$ and is not a generator.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
In general the group $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ is always cyclic, a generator is called a primitive element (primitive root modulo $p$). This is the basis of Diffie–Hellman and the discrete logarithm.

exercises.title: Field Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ is a field extension of degree 4 over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Basis of the Extension
$\{1,\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{6}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

Step 2: Linear Independence
Suppose $a + b\sqrt{2} + c\sqrt{3} + d\sqrt{6} = 0$.
Then $a^2 + 2b^2 + 3c^2 + 6d^2 + 2\sqrt{6}(ad + bc) = 0$.
This contradicts the irrationality of $\sqrt{6}$.

Step 3: Generating System
Every element can be expressed as a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination.

Step 4: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3}):\mathbb{Q}] = 4$.

exercises.title: Characteristic
exercises.description: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Show that the map $\varphi: K \rightarrow K$ with $\varphi(x) = x^p$ is a field homomorphism (Frobenius homomorphism).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Additivity
$(x+y)^p = x^p + y^p$ in characteristic $p$.
Proof via binomial coefficients.

Step 2: Multiplicativity
$(xy)^p = x^p y^p$.
Follows from commutativity.

Step 3: Injectivity
$\ker(\varphi) = \{0\}$.
Since $K$ is a field.

Step 4: Conclusion
$\varphi$ is an injective field homomorphism.

exercises.title: Complex Field Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)$ is a field extension of degree 6 over $\mathbb{Q}$, where $\omega$ is a primitive third root of unity.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Minimal Polynomials
$\sqrt[3]{2}$ has minimal polynomial $X^3 - 2$.
$\omega$ has minimal polynomial $X^2 + X + 1$.

Step 2: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$.
$[\mathbb{Q}(\omega):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$.

Step 3: Basis
$\{1,\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{4},\omega,\omega\sqrt[3]{2},\omega\sqrt[3]{4}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

Step 4: Conclusion
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega):\mathbb{Q}] = 6$.

exercises.title: Complex Algebraic Extensions
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[5]{2})$ is an algebraic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ and determine the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[5]{2}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Minimal Polynomial
$f(X) = X^5 - 2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[5]{2}$.

Step 2: Irreducibility
By the Eisenstein criterion with $p=2$, $f$ is irreducible.

Step 3: Degree of the Extension
$[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[5]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 5$.

Step 4: Basis
$\{1,\sqrt[5]{2},\sqrt[5]{4},\sqrt[5]{8},\sqrt[5]{16}\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis.

exercises.title: Complex Field Homomorphisms
exercises.description: Determine all field homomorphisms from $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ to $\mathbb{C}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Minimal Polynomial
$X^3 - 2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2}$.

Step 2: Roots
The roots are $\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}$.

Step 3: Homomorphisms
$\varphi_1(\sqrt[3]{2}) = \sqrt[3]{2}$.
$\varphi_2(\sqrt[3]{2}) = \omega\sqrt[3]{2}$.
$\varphi_3(\sqrt[3]{2}) = \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}$.

Step 4: Conclusion
There are exactly three field homomorphisms.

exercises.title: Complex Characteristic and Frobenius
exercises.description: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Show that the Frobenius homomorphism $\varphi: K \rightarrow K$ with $\varphi(x) = x^p$ is a field automorphism if $K$ is finite.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Homomorphism
$\varphi$ is a field homomorphism.

Step 2: Injectivity
$\ker(\varphi) = \{0\}$.
Since $K$ is a field.

Step 3: Surjectivity
$K$ is finite.
$\varphi$ is injective.
Thus, $\varphi$ is surjective.

Step 4: Conclusion
$\varphi$ is a field automorphism.

exercises.title: Complex Field Extensions and Galois Groups
exercises.description: Determine the Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Automorphisms
$\sigma(\sqrt{2}) = \pm\sqrt{2}$.
$\sigma(\sqrt{3}) = \pm\sqrt{3}$.

Step 2: Galois Group
$\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})/\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$.

Step 3: Verification
The automorphisms are:
$\sigma_1: \sqrt{2} \mapsto \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \mapsto \sqrt{3}$.
$\sigma_2: \sqrt{2} \mapsto -\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \mapsto \sqrt{3}$.
$\sigma_3: \sqrt{2} \mapsto \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \mapsto -\sqrt{3}$.
$\sigma_4: \sqrt{2} \mapsto -\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3} \mapsto -\sqrt{3}$.

Step 4: Conclusion
The Galois group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$.

exercises.title: Complex Finite Fields and Polynomials
exercises.description: Show that $X^4 + X + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and construct a field with 16 elements.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Irreducibility
$X^4 + X + 1$ has no roots in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
$X^4 + X + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

Step 2: Construction
$\mathbb{F}_{16} = \mathbb{Z}_2[X]/(X^4 + X + 1)$.

Step 3: Elements
$\{a + bX + cX^2 + dX^3 \mid a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Z}_2\}$.

Step 4: Verification
$\mathbb{F}_{16}$ is a field with 16 elements.

exercises.title: Complex Field Homomorphisms and Automorphisms
exercises.description: Determine the automorphism group of $\mathbb{F}_8$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Construction
$\mathbb{F}_8 = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(X^3 + X + 1)$.

Step 2: Automorphisms
$\varphi: X \mapsto X^2$.
$\varphi^2: X \mapsto X^4 = X$.
$\varphi^3 = \text{id}$.

Step 3: Group Structure
$\text{Aut}(\mathbb{F}_8/\mathbb{F}_2) \cong \mathbb{Z}_3$.

Step 4: Conclusion
The automorphism group is cyclic of order 3.

exercises.title: Complex Field Extensions and Galois Groups
exercises.description: Determine the Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, where $\omega$ is a primitive third root of unity.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Automorphisms
$\sigma(\sqrt[3]{2}) \in \{\sqrt[3]{2},\omega\sqrt[3]{2},\omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}\}$.
$\sigma(\omega) \in \{\omega,\omega^2\}$.

Step 2: Galois Group
$\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)/\mathbb{Q}) \cong S_3$.

Step 3: Verification
The automorphisms are:
$\sigma_1: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega$.
$\sigma_2: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \omega\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega$.
$\sigma_3: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega$.
$\sigma_4: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega^2$.
$\sigma_5: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \omega\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega^2$.
$\sigma_6: \sqrt[3]{2} \mapsto \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega \mapsto \omega^2$.

Step 4: Conclusion
The Galois group is isomorphic to $S_3$.
